title: Harvard Law dropout raises $6M for Blue Voice to build a ‘Harvey for police officers’
content:
David Lawrence was a Harvard Law student when an on-campus shooting involving a police officer sparked intense controversy over police conduct. Realizing that most policing errors occur when officers lack instant access to department rules, Lawrence dropped out to tackle the problem with AI. He teamed up with co-founders Amit Patankar, a Harvard MBA and former Google engineer, and Michael Gropman, a retired Boston police deputy chief, to launch Blue Voice — a Boston-based AI startup that provides real-time policy guidance to officers in the field.
Three years later, Blue Voice is coming out of stealth with $6 million in funding led by SignalFire and Las Olas VC. Officers at 225 county agencies across 25 states now rely on the tool daily to ensure their actions follow department protocol — a platform Lawrence likens to Harvey, the AI tool widely used by lawyers, or OpenEvidence, which is a similar tool for doctors.
“When an officer makes a decision, they do so from memory or best guess, based on thousands of pages of law, policy, municipal ordinances, and state laws that they’ve internalized and keep in their head,” Lawrence told TechCrunch.
Before Blue Voice, an officer who couldn’t recall a specific protocol — like the exact seventh step required at a crime scene — had few good options: Flip through a 15,000-page manual, wake up a supervisor in the middle of the night, or search generic tools like Google or ChatGPT that lack police-specific training. The problem was that traditional methods took too much time, while consumer AI models delivered incorrect answers up to 30% of the time, Lawrence said.
Blue Voice says it solves this issue because it is trained on department-specific laws, local ordinances, protocols, and guidelines that general-purpose AI tools can’t access on the public internet. The platform also gives officers instant access to detailed school maps on their phones during active-shooter emergencies.
Today, Blue Voice answers a question every minute. Lawrence says that officers feel confident relying on the tool because it always points them directly to original regulations rather than just generating an answer on its own the way ChatGPT would. Rather than dictating actions, the tool simply provides the laws, leaving the final decision to the officers, who combine it with their own field experience.
Over the last year, says Lawrence, Blue Voice grew its customer base elevenfold because police departments see concrete results, including reduced crime and fewer operational controversies.
Blue Voice recently helped prevent a kidnapping after a rookie officer spotted a man pressuring a young girl to enter his vehicle, according to Lawrence. Unsure whether he had legal grounds to intervene, the officer consulted Blue Voice on his phone. The app instantly confirmed that the situation met the legal criteria for “child enticement” — an offense covering attempts to lure a minor for the purpose of committing a crime against them — giving him the immediate authority to act.
In another instance, Blue Voice reminded a department chief that he couldn’t return an officer to active-duty following a shooting without first obtaining a third-party mental health evaluation.
The startup, which competes with PE-backed Lexipol, also recently developed functionality to help detectives solve cold cases.
At a time when police use of AI — such as Flock Safety’s license plate surveillance systems — draws growing criticism, Lawrence hopes Blue Voice proves that properly deployed AI can deliver public safety benefits without sacrificing civil rights.
Lawrence, who previously worked for Connecticut governor Ned Lamont, developed a deep passion for public service and says he has no regrets about leaving law school behind. “This is the best thing I could do with my career and the most impact I could potentially make,” he said.
Above, left to right: Michael Gropman, David Lawrence, and Amit Patankar.

report.summary: Blue Voice raises $6M to provide police with real-time, department-specific AI policy guidance, aiming to reduce errors and improve public safety.
report.background: David Lawrence was a Harvard Law student when an on-campus police shooting sparked intense controversy. He realized officers often make mistakes because they lack instant access to department rules. Dropping out, he teamed with a former Google engineer and a retired Boston police deputy chief to launch Blue Voice. The Boston startup trains its AI on department-specific laws, ordinances, and protocols that general-purpose tools like ChatGPT cannot access. After three years in stealth, it emerged with $6M in funding from SignalFire and Las Olas VC. Officers at 225 county agencies across 25 states now use the tool daily. It answers a question every minute and competes with PE-backed Lexipol. Lawrence believes properly deployed AI can deliver public safety benefits without sacrificing civil rights.
key_points: Blue Voice has raised $6 million in funding led by SignalFire and Las Olas VC, and has grown its customer base elevenfold over the past year. It currently serves 225 county agencies across 25 states, signaling strong demand from police departments looking for specialized AI tools.

The tool solves a real operational problem: officers previously had to flip through 15,000-page manuals, wake supervisors, or rely on generic AI that gave incorrect answers up to 30% of the time. Blue Voice provides instant, department-specific answers drawn from local laws and protocols.

Unlike ChatGPT, Blue Voice does not simply generate an answer. It points officers directly to the original regulations, allowing them to verify the source. The final decision remains with the officer, who combines the AI guidance with field experience and judgment.

Real-world examples include preventing a kidnapping by confirming legal grounds for child enticement, and reminding a chief that an officer needed a mental health evaluation before returning to duty after a shooting. The startup is also developing cold-case-solving features.

Blue Voice enters a charged environment where police AI like Flock Safety’s license plate surveillance draws criticism. The company positions itself as a civil-rights-friendly alternative because it informs officers rather than surveilling civilians, though oversight concerns remain.
report.impact: Blue Voice represents a shift toward vertical-specific AI that augments professional decision-making rather than replacing it. For the AI industry, it validates the market for fine-tuned, source-cited tools trained on private or restricted data—similar to Harvey for lawyers and OpenEvidence for doctors. Developers can learn from its RAG-style approach: grounding outputs in original documents to prevent hallucinations and build trust. For police departments, it offers a way to reduce procedural errors and operational controversies. For everyday citizens, the upside is fairer, more consistent policing and potentially safer outcomes in emergencies. However, it also raises important questions about accountability, bias in underlying policies, and whether AI guidance could be misused to justify questionable actions. The company’s success may encourage more startups to build narrowly-scoped AI for public institutions, but only if they can maintain transparency and independent oversight.
report.tools: Watch Blue Voice’s approach alongside Harvey (legal AI) and OpenEvidence (medical AI) as domain-specific assistants. For developers interested in similar tools, explore open-source RAG frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex to build question-answering systems grounded in official documents. Lexipol is the main commercial competitor to study. Also monitor Flock Safety for contrast in how AI is applied to policing, and follow MITRE’s or NIST’s AI risk frameworks for responsible deployment guidance.
